title: One word of peace
hookLine: better than a thousand empty words is one word that brings peace (Dhammapada 100)
tomorrow: what's the biggest win a person can have?

cards: It's after midnight, and the version to a friend is now four screens long. Every paragraph explains one more thing you meant. That's where Zoe is with Theo, thumb over send.

The Dhammapada has a chapter called the Thousands, and it opens with a verse about exactly this. Better than a thousand words with no sense in them, it says, is one word that brings peace to the one who hears it.

teach.b: The commentary tells the story behind that verse. A man served the king as an executioner for many years.
On the day he finally stopped, he made himself a bowl of sweet milk-rice, and just then the monk Sariputta came by on his alms round. The man offered him the rice.
Sariputta began to teach, but the man couldn't hear a word; his mind kept going back to what his hands had done.

teach.h: A FEW GENTLE WORDS, THEN QUIET.
teach.b: Sariputta saw it, and spoke to that first, a few gentle words, until the man grew quiet. Only then could the teaching land.
Later the monks wondered how so little could do so much, and the Buddha answered with the verse: one word that brings peace.

Buddhists have a name for what Sariputta did: right speech, a step on the Buddha's Eightfold Path. In one sutta the Buddha says he speaks only what is true and beneficial, and he knows the right time to say it.
The right one, when it can be heard. Four screens of explaining can be more for the writer. One true sentence is for the reader.

how: Right speech (samma vaca) is one step of the Buddha's Eightfold Path; Buddhists describe it as speech that is true, kind, helpful and timely, and lay Buddhists take a precept against false speech.

games.q: what does “one word of peace” mean?
o: keeping silent for a whole day as a vow
a few true words that quiet the person who hears them
a short blessing chanted over a sleeping child

games.q: the story behind verse 100: tap the pairs.
p: offered milk-rice on his last day
spoke gently to the trouble first
true, beneficial, at the right time

s: right speech is a step on the Buddha's Eightfold Path
speech is part of the path itself, beside right action and right livelihood.
the more fully you explain yourself, the more peace it brings
the verse prizes one word that quiets the hearer over a thousand empty ones.
in the story, Sariputta's long teaching changed the man at once
he couldn't hear it until a few gentle words quieted his mind first.

games.q: you're Sariputta. you've started teaching, but the man in front of you isn't hearing a word; he's lost in his past. what do you do?
o: keep teaching; the words will reach him eventually.
speak gently to what's troubling him first, then teach.
leave and come back on a better day.
games.why: Sariputta met the trouble first. a few words brought quiet, and then the teaching could land. one word of peace.

practice: Think of one person who could use a word of peace from you today. Write them one short, true sentence: thank you, I'm sorry, or I'm glad you're here.
Hold it through the sit without sending, and read it once more at the end, cutting any word it doesn't need.

wordCard.voice: One word of peace: the Dhammapada's word that quiets the hearer, worth more than a thousand empty ones. Right speech, said when it can land.

carryVoice: Hold on to this: one word of peace, at the right time. Five days with the Dhammapada now.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 100 (the Thousands: one word that brings peace is better than a thousand senseless ones)
Dhammapada Commentary on verse 100: the executioner Tambadathika and Sariputta (cf. Burlingame, Buddhist Legends, 1921)
Majjhima Nikaya 58, Abhayarajakumara Sutta (the Buddha speaks what is true and beneficial, knowing the right time)
Samyutta Nikaya 45.8 (the Eightfold Path; right speech defined)
